REQ-M3-007, WP-104 (RSK-026; ADR-0013 decision 9): after a request times out the virtio-blk driver publishes nothing more to the device. Every request shares one header, one status byte, one data buffer and the same three descriptors, and a completion is taken by its position in the used ring, so a request the driver gave up could still complete later and be taken for the next one, and a later write's bytes could reach the earlier request's sector. The case reads one pattern sector (before=ok, pattern=1: the shared buffer now holds that sector), fills its own buffer with a guard byte and arms the test kernel's hook, which withholds the next request from the device (not published, no notify) and shortens its wait so the driver's own timeout branch runs: that read answers K_E_BLK_TIMEOUT, and the block layer writes the line `kernel|blk|stopped|op=read|sector=131064|code=K_E_BLK_TIMEOUT`, once in the whole run (max_counts: the four refusals after it write none). Then four requests are each refused with K_E_BLK_NEEDS_RESET: a read of the timed-out request's sector, a write to that sector of the bytes it already holds, a flush, and a read past the end of the device (refused as stopped, not as out of range). The caller's buffer keeps the guard after the timed-out read and the refused read (caller_kept=1: these two failed reads hand back nothing); after the refused write the shared buffer still holds the first sector (buffer_kept=1: the refusal comes before the copy); the driver's available index did not move across the four refusals (published=0); no frame is left; exit 33. Not shown by this case: a late completion from a real device (the withheld request never reaches the device); the order of the refusal against the missing-FLUSH shortcut (the lab device offers FLUSH); that the stop lasts beyond these four requests (the flag is never cleared: read in the code, not measured).
